docs.title: FortranCallJulia
docs.text:
Embed the Julia runtime inside a Fortran application: Fortran calls Julia through a C bridge (the fcj_* C ABI), and Julia solvers call back into Fortran – one process, zero-copy arrays, every call exception-checked.

Start with the four introduction pages:

  • What is FortranCallJulia? – the 30-second tour
  • Why Fortran and Julia? – the motivation and the split of labor
  • Architecture – the three worlds, with the interactive diagram
  • Validation – the three hard metrics and where they come from

Ready to build? Continue with Installation.

Bilingual site

This documentation ships in English and 简体中文. Use the language selector in the top bar to switch.

docs.title: Acceptance gates
docs.text:
The bridge is correct when it reproduces a native computation. That claim is checked, not asserted: a set of example executables compare bridge-computed results against native references and print loud PASS sentinels, exiting nonzero on failure. There is no ctest wiring (Known limitations) – the gates are run by hand, and this page is the runner’s manual: what each gate checks, how to run it, and the one way the whole procedure silently lies to you (a version-skewed baseline).

What the gates mean physically is told on the Validation page; here we keep the mechanics and the maintenance discipline.

docs.title: The gate inventory
docs.text:
Sentinel Example Checks SOD_VALIDATION_PASS 07_capstone/1_reacting_flow.f90 (sod mode) Sod tube vs the exact Riemann solution DETONATION_VALIDATION_PASS 07_capstone/1_reacting_flow.f90 (detonation mode) CJ detonation speed vs the analytic Chapman–Jouguet value EX_CAPSTONE_GRI_IGNITION_PASS 07_capstone/2_gri_ignition.f90 four gated quantities vs the native Julia run (below) DEMO_PASS 06_sciml/3_sciml_demo.f90 the SciML callback demo end to end

The detonation gate is the headline physics check: at nx = 2700 the computed front speed is 7.12391 against the analytic CJ speed 7.12470 – a deviation of 0.011%, with the burned state within 0.025% of CJ (u 0.025%, p 0.023%, rho 0.018%). (At nx = 400 the same gate fails loudly at +8.53% and says so: under-resolution is an error, not a pass.)

docs.title: The four-quantity GRI gate
docs.text:
2_gri_ignition.f90 gates not one number but four, all at the same tolerance – the ignition delay t_ign (1.1075 ms), the end temperature T_end, and two mole-fraction spot values chosen because they pin the layout-sensitive 4 x 2001 column-major matrix extraction (CH4 at t = 0, CO2 at t_end). The verdict block, verbatim from examples/07_capstone/2_gri_ignition.f90:

    rel = abs(t_ign_f - t_ign_nat) / t_ign_nat
    rel_t = abs(T(NSAMPLE) - t_end_nat) / t_end_nat
    rel_x1 = abs(x_at(1, 1) - x_ch4_nat) / x_ch4_nat
    rel_x2 = abs(x_at(3, NSAMPLE) - x_co2_nat) / x_co2_nat
    ...
    if (rel < REL_TOL .and. rel_t < REL_TOL .and. rel_x1 < REL_TOL &
        .and. rel_x2 < REL_TOL) then
        print *, 'EX_CAPSTONE_GRI_IGNITION_PASS'

with REL_TOL = 1.0e-8_c_double. Under a correctly pinned runtime the four deviations are exactly 0, and the full-trajectory overlay audit puts the worst series residual below 1e-12 (measured ~8.3e-13, on the steepest CO2 rise). The two X gates are the layout tripwire: if the column-major flattening were ever off, X(1,1) reads the wrong species and the gate fails by orders of magnitude, not marginally.

Note what is gated: converged scalars, not pointwise trajectories. Two independent solves of the same stiff system differ in last-bit fashion across a handful of transition points even on one runtime, so a pointwise gate would flake; the four scalars are stable. The gates are tight enough that a wrong runtime cannot sneak through – which is the next section.

docs.title: Running the gates
docs.text:
Build with examples on, then generate the native baseline before running the bridge side. The recipe from the header of examples/07_capstone/2_gri_ignition.f90 (the Julia path below is a placeholder – use your pinned 1.12.7 binary, not a version shim):

    cd build/examples
    <pinned-julia-1.12.7>/bin/julia --project=../../scripts/sysimage_env \
        ../../examples/07_capstone/run_gri_native.jl
    ./ex_capstone_gri_ignition

The baseline script writes gri_native.dat (the four reference values) and the full native trajectory output/gri_native_series.csv; the executable reads the .dat, runs the identical FjKinetics call path through the bridge, extracts the arrays, and prints the four relative differences plus the sentinel. The other gates need no baseline step – their references are analytic or built in.

A stale baseline is caught loudly: the executable refuses a .dat whose format does not match the current script, with a “regenerate” hint.

docs.title: The trap: a drifting baseline fails the gates and blames the bridge
docs.text:
The acceptance comparison is only meaningful if both sides run the same Julia. The bridge executable embeds the build-pinned libjulia 1.12.7; the native baseline is generated by whatever julia is on the path. On a machine where that julia is an auto-updating version shim, the pair silently skews – and the failure mode is nasty: the gates report the bridge’s extraction as the suspect, because the bridge is the side being tested.

This is not hypothetical; it happened. A baseline regenerated under a shim pointing at 1.13.2 left two of the four gates showing nonzero margins (0 / 1.74e-9 / 0 / 6.75e-9, the worst 6.75e-9) – apparently passing, actually poisoned – and on the transition window the pointwise drift reached T rel 1.5e-5 and CH4 rel 0.54. The 1e-8 door was being crossed by a baseline skew, while the investigation initially chased solver nondeterminism and thread ordering. Re-generating the baseline with the pinned binary turned all four deviations into exact zeros overnight. The full story is on Lessons; the engineering residue is two guards.

The runtime guard, verbatim from examples/07_capstone/run_gri_native.jl (the original error string names the developer’s install path; shortened here to the placeholder):

const BRIDGE_JULIA = v"1.12.7"   # the libjulia the bridge executable links
VERSION == BRIDGE_JULIA || error(
    "native baseline must be generated with the bridge-pinned Julia " *
    "$BRIDGE_JULIA (this is $(VERSION)) -- use the pinned 1.12.7 binary, " *
    "not the juliaup shim. A different runtime drifts at the ignition " *
    "transition and fails the 1e-8 gates while wrongly indicting the " *
    "bridge extraction.")

The build-side twin is the FJ_BUILD_SYSIMAGE guard in CMakeLists.txt, which rejects any Julia outside the 1.12.x line at configure time and says so (“do not use the juliaup shim”).

docs.title: Maintenance discipline
docs.text:
1. Regenerate the baseline with the pinned binary, every time. The guard makes any other choice loud.
  2. After any bridge change, run all four gates, not just the one nearest your change. A past review fix introduced a regression that only the newly added X gates caught – the t_ign gate alone had been passing over a doubly-indirect species indexing bug.
  3. Watch the margins, not just the sentinel. The gate prints the four deviations; exact zeros are the healthy steady state. Anything consistently at 1e-9 means the baseline pair is skewed again – find the runtime before touching the bridge.

docs.title: Performance annex
docs.text:
This annex is published in English only.

Migrated from examples/07_capstone/PERFORMANCE.md (the 2026-10-26 capstone report). Every number, table, and conclusion below is reproduced verbatim; only the prose identifying the measurement machines has been genericized for the public site (machine references read “a shared build host” / “the loaded host” here – load figures and core counts are part of the measurement record and are unchanged).

docs.title: Capstone performance report: Fortran ⇄ Julia reacting-flow example
docs.text: All numbers from the 2026-10-26 runs on a shared build host (192-core, load ~119 during measurement; single core per run). Julia 1.12.7, FjKinetics on the compat-pinned stack: the load-bearing pins (OrdinaryDiffEq 6.111.0, Catalyst 16.2.1, PrecompileTools 1.3.4) are identical in every validation environment; patch-level deps differ slightly by artifact – the JIT runs resolved through FjKinetics’ Manifest at measurement time (SciMLBase 2.155.1, StaticArrays 1.9.18), while the sysimage and AOT environments resolved SciMLBase 2.155.2 / StaticArrays 1.9.24 (within [compat], which floors the minor lines, so the 700x drift class cannot recur through resolution). Identical compiled kernel (FjKinetics.step_chemistry!, Rodas5P, abstol 1e-10 / reltol 1e-8) in every mode.

docs.title: End-to-end detonation validation (HLW 2000 Ex.2, nx = 2700, t = 0.3)
docs.text:
The Fortran driver owns the time loop (2608 transport steps, 5216 Strang chemistry half-steps, 25245 active cell-solves). Physics identical in both modes: detonation speed 7.12391 vs s_CJ = 7.12470 (0.011%), burnt state within 0.025% of CJ (worst: u 0.025%, p 0.023%, rho 0.018%).

mode julia init first non-empty chem call chemistry total run total peak RSS bridge calls jit (project env) 17.3 s 7.58 ms 4.79 s 7.72 s 1.15 GB 5231 sysimage 1.90 s 8.04 ms 4.02 s 7.04 s 1.18 GB 5229

Final driver (post round-2 review fixes), 2026-10-26, back-to-back runs from the repo root; the build/examples-cwd repeats gave jit 15.7 s / 7.11 ms / 4.43 s / 7.22 s and sysimage 0.96 s / 7.83 ms / 4.99 s / 7.95 s. Bridge calls = init/setup + 5215 chemistry (one julia_eval per half-step with a nonempty active set) + 1 shutdown; init/setup is 15 in jit mode (binding probe + import FjKinetics + re-probe) vs 13 in sysimage mode (probe only — the image binds Main.FjKinetics already, so no import runs). Peak RSS from the earlier same-day batch (VmHWM poller); the fixes touch only setup and validation, not the measured paths. Init ranges across all same-day runs: jit 15.1-20.2 s (loading ~92 package caches; the high end under load), sysimage 0.93-2.37 s (the low end with a warm page cache).

Zero-JIT verification (corrected after adversarial review). An earlier revision of this report timed “the first chemistry half-step” at 21.6/21.8 µs and called that the zero-JIT proof. That was an empty measurement: half-step 1 has an empty active set (unburnt cells sit below t_cut, burnt driver cells below z_floor), so it makes no Julia call at all and the timer covered only the 2700-cell packing loop. The probe now clocks the first NON-EMPTY half-step — the post-transport one, the first call that actually crosses the bridge. Result on the final driver: 7.1-8.0 ms across all four runs (jit 7.58/7.11 ms, sysimage 8.04/7.83 ms) — statistically indistinguishable, all ms-scale, i.e. pure solver work over the handful of newly-shocked cells. A runtime compile event would cost 100 ms-seconds; no run shows one. The jit mode’s ms-scale first call is a package-cache hit (FjKinetics’ PrecompileTools workload precompiled the exact view-based call signature), the sysimage’s is the same code baked in the image. Per-active-cell-solve: jit 4.79/4.43 s per 25245 = 175-190 µs, sysimage 4.02/4.99 s per 25245 = 159-198 µs — the ranges overlap, and the direction of the difference flips WITHIN this batch (repo-root runs: sysimage 4.02 < jit 4.79; build-cwd runs: sysimage 4.99 > jit 4.43) and again across earlier same-day batches (4.10 vs 4.87, then 4.60 vs 3.89) — the jit-vs-sysimage chemistry-total gap is host-load noise (~±20%), not a mode effect.

docs.title: Chemistry kernel micro-benchmark (identical 64-cell hot/frozen mix)
docs.text:
chem_bench_reference.jl (pure Julia) and 3_aot_kinetics/ (standalone compiled library) drive the same interleaved workload: odd cells at T = 17 (full 10-decade burn, ~100 internal steps each), even cells at T = 1.6 (frozen, one internal step), dt = 4e-4, state reset every call.

mode startup steady per cell-step pure Julia (package caches, JIT) 17.5 s load 309 µs embedded jit / sysimage (from the detonation run above) (see above) 190 / 159 µs (batch ranges 175-190 / 159-198 µs) AOT standalone library 0.58-1.97 s init** 236 / 347 / 319 / 240 / 240 / 191 / 353 / 361 µs (eight runs, three builds)

Per-cell-step costs are accuracy-driven (Rodas5P resolving F through 10 decades at reltol 1e-8): ~6 µs frozen, ~65 µs induction, ~430 µs burn on an idle core (measured 2026-10-26, bench2); the mixed-workload figures above are on the loaded host (~±20% run-to-run). The per-half-step bridge eval adds only parse cost (µs), dwarfed by the ~180 µs/cell of solver work in the real run.

** AOT init spans 0.58-1.97 s across runs: cold page cache on the 1.5 GB library vs warm; the cold-machine bound is the high end. The eight steady numbers span three library builds (original; round-1 guarded @ccallables; round-2 clearable-solver + init) and two allocation shapes: 191 µs was measured inside a 32-core allocation (dedicated physical cores); 353/361 µs come from 1-core allocations on the loaded host, where a hyperthread sibling of the lone core is busy (the 2x gap tracks the sibling, not the build). The per-build triplets agree within the host-load band — the guards never touch the hot path.

docs.title: What each mode buys
docs.text:
• JIT (embedded, project env): zero build steps, slowest startup (~15-20 s), needs the full depot on the target machine.
  • sysimage: one 1.20 GB image; startup 2.4 s (6-8×); same heap footprint (peak RSS within 30 MB of JIT); no compilation risk at runtime by construction.
  • AOT library: fastest startup (0.58-1.97 s library init, cold- to warm-cache — plain image load, no package caches, no env); no Julia installation, depot, or project on the target, kernel reached by C symbols (kinetics_build, kinetics_step, zero-copy unsafe_wrap of the Fortran buffers; error-code contract — no Julia exception can cross the C ABI, and a fresh library load starts WITHOUT a solver: a module init clears the build-time solver at image load, so kinetics_step before kinetics_build returns -2 instead of silently computing with baked-in parameters). One-time build cost: 50 min wall and ~33 GB peak compiler RSS for the non-incremental codegen of the whole dependency closure (this is build-machine memory, not deployment footprint); dist/ 2.5 GB with the lazy MKL artifacts bundled (1.8 GB before, see incident below). Build + guards + first batched 64-cell step after init is 14-25 ms, and the first timed step (post-warm-up) 14-19 ms ≈ steady — no compilation at runtime; the error codes (-2 before build, -1 bad n, 0 success) are exercised by built-in guards on every bench run, including in the empty-depot proof environment.

docs.title: Version-pinning incident (why the pinned stack matters)
docs.text: Measured 2026-10-26: with the same example resolved against OrdinaryDiffEq 7.8.1 (the unpinned float), the per-cell reinit!/step! pattern degrades ~700× — a frozen cell costs 982 internal steps instead of 1, a burning cell ~50 000 instead of ~100, ~3.5 MB allocated per cell — turning the nx=2700 chemistry budget into hours. FjKinetics pins its tested line in [compat]; the sysimage and AOT environments resolve through it.

docs.title: First-init artifact downloads (self-containedness)
docs.text: The very first AOT run downloaded ~570 MB from the network at init_julia (IntelOpenMP, oneTBB, MKL) before touching any chemistry: LinearSolve, deep in the SciML closure, probes the MKL_jll lazy artifact when the image loads, and PackageCompiler bundles only non-lazy artifacts by default — so the “standalone” library silently reached for the internet on any machine without a Julia depot. Fix: create_library(...; include_lazy_artifacts = true) bakes the lazy artifacts into dist/ (verified with an empty JULIA_DEPOT_PATH and fresh HOME: no downloads, bench green — re-proven on every guarded rebuild, most recently the final round-2 artifact). The 283 s first-init measurement is that download run; 0.58-1.97 s is init with the artifacts resolved locally.

docs.title: Bridge internals
docs.text:
Eight C files, four responsibility groups, one contract. The user-facing pages describe the bridge from outside – the fcj_* ABI, the two Fortran SDK layers, the numbers. This page opens the box: what each file owns, how the GC debt is paid, and where the Julia 1.12 C API forced workarounds. It is written for maintainers changing src/bridge/; nothing here is needed to use the bridge.

The architecture page gives the same system in one screen; read that first if you are new.

docs.title: The eight files
docs.text:
Group Files Owns Core core.c, memory.c lifecycle (fcj_init / fcj_init_ex / fcj_shutdown), thread pinning, the GC root set Dispatch & boxing dispatch.c, types.c fcj_call* / fcj_call_kwargs, the function-name cache, scalar boxing (fcj_box_*) Array channel arrays.c, extract.c N-D zero-copy wraps, deep copies, batch extraction to Fortran Callback access callbacks.c, accessors.c @cfunction trampolines, get_field / get_property, native Float64 element access

Two headers frame them. bridge.h is the public contract: 53 fcj_ functions plus fcj_options_t – everything a Fortran bind(c) layer can reach. bridge_internal.h is private: the native element accessors (fcj_get_real and siblings), shared helpers, and the per-module cache-clear hooks fcj_shutdown walks. The “~105 exported fcj_* symbols” headline used across this site counts the whole fcj_ namespace across these sources; the binding layer src/julia_binding.f90 declares 58 of them (52 of the 53 public functions – fcj_ready is never bound – plus the 6 internal element accessors), and the rest are internal helpers that never cross the ABI.

docs.title: Core: lifecycle and the root set
docs.text:
core.c owns the state machine. fcj_state is _Atomic; every entry point checks it through fcj_ready() before touching Julia. The thread rule from Known limitations is enforced, not documented, in check_thread() (verbatim from src/bridge/core.c):

int check_thread() {
    if (pthread_self() != main_thread_id) {
        char msg[256];
        snprintf(msg, sizeof(msg), "Thread Error: Julia called from thread %p, runtime owned by thread %p",
                 (void*)pthread_self(), (void*)main_thread_id);
        set_error(msg);
        return 0; // Fail
    }
    return 1; // OK
}

Failure semantics split by entry point: fcj_init aborts the process on failure (the original contract), while fcj_init_ex returns an error code and leaves the reason in fcj_get_last_error() – surfaced in Fortran as get_last_error_message(). fcj_shutdown is one-way: the state machine never returns to READY, and re-initialization after shutdown is rejected loudly rather than attempted.

memory.c is the GC story, and its header comment states the design better than a paraphrase would (from src/bridge/memory.c):

// fcj_retain/fcj_release keep their bind(C) signatures but no longer round-trip
// through Julia (retain_obj/release_obj in GCManager.jl) on the hot path.
// Retained objects live in a Julia Vector{Any} reachable through the constant
// binding `Main.FJ_ROOTS` ... bookkeeping is a pure-C ptr -> slot hash map with
// per-pointer refcounts, mirroring GCManager's REF_COUNTS/PTR_CACHE logic.

The mechanics that matter to a maintainer:

  • A C static is not a GC root. Any function or value cached in a static must be routed through fcj_retain (a module binding counts; a bare static does not). The one sanctioned exception is immortal singletons kept alive by their Base binding, such as the ComplexF64 type object cached in types.c.
  • fcj_map is open-addressing with tombstones and refcounts – deleted entries tombstone so probe chains stay intact, and a pointer retained twice occupies one slot with a count of two.
  • No locking anywhere in these statics. The single-thread contract (check_thread) is the lock. Break the contract and you have a data race, not a bug report.

docs.title: Dispatch and boxing
docs.text:
dispatch.c turns names into calls. The function-name cache is a fixed 256-slot table hashed with FNV-1a; cache hits are routed through fcj_retain so the cached jl_function_t* is rooted. Two invalidation rules a maintainer must never undo:

  1. The cache is cleared first in fcj_shutdown – before anything else could still dereference it.
  2. Every julia_eval_string invalidates the name caches. An eval can redefine f from a function to a closure, and a stale cache entry would call the captured old object forever. (The Fast Path registry keeps its captured-object semantics by design and documents it; see Two SDKs, two speeds.)

fcj_call1_float64 through the N-argument family and fcj_call_kwargs (the keyword-argument path) all funnel through the same jl_call/exception-check tail. types.c boxes Fortran scalars into Julia objects – fcj_box_float64, fcj_box_string, and the rest – plus the cached ComplexF64 datatype noted above.

docs.title: The array channel
docs.text:
arrays.c wraps Fortran memory as a Julia Array of any rank 1 through FCJ_MAX_NDIM, zero-copy, via jl_ptr_to_array. The wrap path, verbatim from src/bridge/arrays.c (the three guard helpers are the same shape, elided for length):

void* fcj_wrap_array(void* data, long ndim, const long* dims) {
    if (!fcj_ready()) { set_error("Julia runtime not initialized or already shut down"); return NULL; }
    if (!check_thread()) return NULL;
    jl_value_t *array_type = NULL;
    jl_value_t *dims_tuple = NULL;
    JL_GC_PUSH2(&array_type, &dims_tuple);

    array_type = array_type_for_ndim(ndim, "fcj_wrap_array");
    ...
    dims_tuple = make_dims_tuple(ndim, dims, "fcj_wrap_array");
    ...
    jl_array_t *arr = jl_ptr_to_array(array_type, data, dims_tuple, 0);

    if (check_julia_exception()) { JL_GC_POP(); return NULL; }
    JL_GC_POP();
    return (void*)arr;
}

Two disciplines visible in that excerpt, both load-bearing everywhere in the bridge: local values are rooted with JL_GC_PUSH2 for the duration of a call, and any error path set_errors a reason before returning NULL. The deep-copy sibling fcj_copy_array allocates a fresh Julia array and memcpys in, with an overflow-checked extent product before the allocation.

extract.c is the return leg: fcj_to_fortran (one bulk copy into a Fortran buffer, length-checked), fcj_get_element, fcj_get_property. The bulk path is a single memcpy from jl_array_data_ with an n == len check – which is why the extraction channel is bit-exact and why the acceptance gates can put a 1e-8 door in front of it (acceptance gates).

docs.title: Callback access
docs.text:
callbacks.c runs the other direction: Fortran bind(c) subroutines wrapped into Julia-callable objects through @cfunction trampolines, with the calling context carried opaquely. This is the machinery behind the OrdinaryDiffEq callback demos of examples/06_sciml/1_callback.f90. The hard rule from the user pages holds at this level too: a trampoline frame cannot host a Julia exception, so a throwing callee is undefined behavior – validate on the Fortran side, return sentinels.

accessors.c implements %element and %property, and here the Julia 1.12 C API forced the most instructive workarounds in the tree. The header of extract.c records them (from src/bridge/extract.c):

// 1.12.7 API notes (verified against include/julia/julia.h):
//  - jl_get_property does not exist; jl_get_field exists but only reads
//    plain struct fields (no getproperty overloads, no NamedTuples), so
//    the contract's fallback applies: Base.getproperty is cached once and
//    jl_call-ed, matching helper_getfield semantics in Accessors.jl;
//    getproperty dispatches on Symbol, so the name is interned with
//    jl_symbol (immortal, globally rooted) instead of boxed as a String;
//  - jl_arrayref does not exist either (removed with the Memory-backed
//    array rewrite), so element boxing goes through a cached
//    Base.getindex binding -- the same numeric boxing jl_arrayref used to
//    perform.

Read that as the general lesson: when a jl_* convenience is missing, cache the equivalent Base function once (rooted through fcj_retain) and jl_call it – do not hand-roll struct offsets. bridge_internal.h adds the native element accessors (fcj_get_real / fcj_set_real and 2- and 3-index forms): direct Float64 reads and writes into wrapped memory, no boxing, used by the hot per-cell paths.

docs.title: Signals and error transport
docs.text:
The bridge never writes jl_options.handle_signals: GC safepoint polling depends on Julia’s own signal handlers, and disabling them crashes at a safepoint – reliably, not occasionally (Lessons). The handle_signals=0 option offered by fcj_options_t means “no takeover”: after a successful init the bridge resets SIGINT/SIGTERM to SIG_DFL, leaving the GC-critical handlers intact.

Errors travel one channel: the per-runtime last-error buffer, read through fcj_get_last_error() and surfaced as get_last_error_message(). A Julia-side exception is caught at the call boundary, formatted into that buffer, and the call returns an invalid handle or NULL – the process keeps running.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: The project is MIT-licensed (LICENSE) – the license is the whole of the legal arrangement; there is no CLA and no contributor agreement beyond it. This page covers the practical half: how to get a working build, what “done” means, and what a good change looks like.

docs.title: Getting to a working build
docs.text: Follow Installation end to end first: a pinned Julia 1.12.x, CMake with examples on, the scratch environment, and a run of the quickstart. Everything on this page assumes that works before you change anything. If it does not build before your change, you have found a bug worth reporting before you write any code.

docs.title: Definition of done: the gates
docs.text:
A change to this repository is done when the gates say so, not when it compiles. In increasing order of cost:

  1. Build clean. CMake configure + build with no new warnings.
  2. Docs gates. .venv-docs/bin/mkdocs build --strict and the parity script must pass with zero warnings – every page exists in both locales, titles are translated, sync stamps agree, and no page leaks machine-specific strings. If you touch any page under docs/, run both.
  3. Acceptance gates. The example gates of acceptance gates, run by hand, sentinel lines green. Bridge or extraction changes owe the full set, not just the nearest example – a past fix shipped a regression that only the layout-sensitivity gates caught.
  4. Rebuild artifacts if your change reaches them. Julia-side package changes invalidate the sysimage and AOT builds (rebuild from zero).

The gates are manual by design (Known limitations). That makes them your job.

docs.title: What a good change looks like
docs.text:
Scoped small, committed in logical units. The repository’s history is written as one commit per logical unit – a feature, its tests, its examples, its docs, its environment changes are separate commits, not one landing. Keep that granularity; it is what makes bisects here actually bisect.

Fail loudly, never silently. The house style is explicit errors with a reason over quiet defaults: invalid handles carry a message readable through get_last_error_message(), stale formats refuse to parse with a regeneration hint, under-resolved runs assert instead of producing plausible-looking wrong numbers. A contribution that adds a silent fallback is working against the codebase.

Match the documented contracts. The public ABI is bridge.h; the Fortran surface is src/julia_binding.f90 and src/julia_sdk.f90; the Julia side is the FortranBridge package. Extending any of them means updating the layer above (and its docs page), not routing around it.

Sanitize anything machine-specific. Examples, scripts, and docs must not hardcode local install paths, hostnames, or usernames – use placeholders, environment overrides, or exe-relative probing, as the existing code does. The docs gates enforce this for prose; hold code and comments to the same bar.

Docs move with the code. User-visible behavior changes update the relevant page in both locales, with the sync stamp advanced. A PR that changes what a gate checks updates acceptance gates in the same commit series.

Ground every claim. Numbers in docs and comments come from the validation runs, with provenance to the script that produced them; if you change a number’s source, change the number. An undocumented measurement is a future person’s wrong assumption.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
Open the PR against the primary branch (main) with:

  • what the change does and why (a linked issue when there is one),
  • which gates you ran and their sentinel output,

docs.title: Lessons
docs.text: Every rule in this codebase was paid for. This page is the receipt drawer: the incidents behind the guards, the pins, and the loud failure modes you will meet while maintaining the bridge. Each entry follows the same shape – symptom, root cause, fix, and the rule left behind. The machines and accounts involved stay anonymous on purpose; the mechanisms are what transfer.

docs.title: 1. Pin the Julia runtime on both sides of any comparison
docs.text:
Symptom. The four GRI acceptance gates (acceptance gates) started reporting nonzero margins around 1e-9 – sometimes passing, sometimes not – on runs where neither the bridge nor the chemistry had changed. The visible suspect was the bridge’s array extraction.

Root cause. A version skew, not a bug. The bridge executable embeds the build-pinned libjulia 1.12.7, but the native baseline had been regenerated with a bare julia that was an auto-updating version shim, silently pointing at 1.13.2 after an upstream release. The same stiff solve, run by two different Julia versions, drifts at the ignition transition – measured pointwise up to T rel 1.5e-5 and CH4 rel 0.54 – which crosses a 1e-8 gate effortlessly. The investigation first chased solver nondeterminism and BLAS thread ordering; re-generating the baseline with the pinned binary produced four exact zeros and closed the case.

Fix. Two guards now refuse the skew loudly: run_gri_native.jl errors unless VERSION == v"1.12.7", and the FJ_BUILD_SYSIMAGE CMake guard rejects any build Julia outside the 1.12.x line, naming the version shim as the thing not to use.

Rule. Any A/B comparison – baseline vs bridge, before vs after – runs the same pinned binary on both sides. When a tight gate flakes, audit the runtimes before the code.

docs.title: 2. Pin the SciML stack with [compat]
docs.text:
Symptom. Per-cell chemistry in the capstone suddenly cost ~700x more: a frozen grid cell took 982 internal integrator steps instead of 1, a burning cell ~54,000 instead of ~100, with ~3.5 MB allocated per cell. At nx = 400 the chemistry phase ran 89 s where the tested stack needed 1.25 s.

Root cause. The scratch environment had drifted onto the OrdinaryDiffEq 7.x line, because the kinetics package carried no [compat] bounds. The 7.x step-size controller handles the per-cell reinit! / step! pattern drastically worse – a dependency resolved “fine”, performing badly.

Fix. The package’s [compat] now pins the tested line – Catalyst ~16.2, OrdinaryDiffEq ~6.111, SciMLBase ~2.155, StaticArrays ~1.9, PrecompileTools ~1.3 – the unused direct ModelingToolkit dependency was dropped, and the environment assembly script documents why the pins are load-bearing.

Rule. Pin everything your numerics depend on, and when throughput degrades for no reason, print the resolved versions before profiling. “Resolves” is not “works”; the resolver optimizes for compatibility, not for your access pattern.

docs.title: 3. Never disable Julia’s signal handling
docs.text:
Symptom. While wiring up startup options, setting jl_options.handle_signals = OFF looked like a clean way to keep an embedded runtime from stealing the host application’s signal handlers. The process then crashed at a GC safepoint – in 14 of 15 runs.

Root cause. Embedded Julia’s GC safepoint polling depends on Julia’s own SIGSEGV handler; turning signal handling off removes machinery the runtime itself needs. The crash is reliable, not racy – which at least makes it easy to reproduce.

Fix. The bridge never writes jl_options.handle_signals. The need it was meant to serve (“don’t take over my signals”) is met differently: handle_signals = 0 in fcj_options_t means no takeover – after a successful init the bridge resets SIGINT / SIGTERM to SIG_DFL, leaving the GC-critical handlers intact.

Rule. Treat jl_options as read-only. If you need host-friendly signal disposition, reset specific signals after init; never remove Julia’s own handlers from under it.

docs.title: 4. On the shared cluster: judge jobs by exit code, not stdout
docs.text:
Symptom. Batch jobs launched through Slurm’s srun on the shared cluster would intermittently print their entire stdout twice – whole blocks duplicated verbatim, across independent runs, on otherwise healthy jobs. Even a bare shell echo reproduced it; no environment variable or node-specific setting explained it.

Root cause. A cluster I/O quirk in the launch layer, not in any program being run. It is noise in the transport, and it cannot be fixed from inside a job.

Fix and rule. Automated verdicts key on the exit code and the test summary line, never on how the log reads; when a log is archived or piped onward, de-duplicate repeated lines (awk '!seen[$0]++' is the house idiom). Never parse a Slurm log for a sentinel you intend to act on without allowing for duplication – and never let a duplicated-looking log convince you a job ran twice.

docs.title: 5. A “self-contained” AOT library that downloads 570 MB on first run
docs.text:
Symptom. A PackageCompiler-built library, advertised as self-contained, spent its first initialization on a network fetch of ~570 MB (IntelOpenMP / oneTBB / MKL) on a machine with no package depot.

Root cause. A dependency in the SciML closure probes MKL_jll – a lazy artifact – at image load. PackageCompiler’s default bundles only non-lazy artifacts, so “everything you need” silently meant “everything except the lazies”.

Fix. Build with include_lazy_artifacts = true; the capstone’s AOT build script carries the comment explaining exactly this. Verified by initializing under an empty JULIA_DEPOT_PATH and a fresh home directory: zero network access.

Rule. “Self-contained” is a testable claim – test it with an empty depot on a network-isolated path, not by reading your own build script.

docs.title: 6. An AOT library owns its runtime: enter through its own front door
docs.text:
Symptom. Linking a compiled Julia library into a process that also uses the bridge SDK worked – until initialization segfaulted or misbehaved in ways that pointed everywhere at once.

Root cause. The compiled library bundles its own libjulia, and the process now has two opinions about where the runtime lives. Calling the SDK’s julia_init() drives a bare jl_init() that looks for a default sys.so the bundled layout does not ship – the sysimage is compiled into the library, and only its exported init_julia knows how to load it, with an explicit bindir.

Fix. In AOT mode, lifecycle goes through the library’s exported init_julia / shutdown_julia and nothing else. The interface declarations live in src/lib_support/julia_library_interface.f90, and the working examples (examples/03_deployment/2_compiled_library/, examples/07_capstone/3_aot_kinetics/) show the pattern.

Rule. One process, one runtime owner. When a library ships its own Julia, that library’s entry points – not the SDK’s – are the lifecycle.

docs.title: Rebuild from zero
docs.text:
Three artifacts in this repository are built products rather than source: the SciML sysimage, the AOT chemistry library, and the capstone figure set. All three can be regenerated from scratch on a fresh clone – this page is the recipe for each, with the guards and flags that keep the rebuild honest. Paths are shown relative to the repository root; wherever a Julia binary is named, use the pinned 1.12.7 install, not a version shim (Lessons, entry 1).

The common prerequisite for the first two is the pinned scratch environment scripts/sysimage_env. scripts/install_sciml_env.jl assembles it (developing FortranBridge and the kinetics packages into it, resolving through the [compat] pins); run it with the same 1.12.x Julia the bridge embeds.

docs.title: Step 1: the SciML sysimage
docs.text:
The sysimage is what turns a 17.3 s JIT startup into a 1.90 s load (deployment modes). Rebuild it whenever the Julia-side packages change shape. Two entry points, one result:

    cmake -B build -DFJ_BUILD_SYSIMAGE=ON ...
    cmake --build build --target fcj_sysimage

The configure step runs the version guard: FJ_BUILD_SYSIMAGE accepts only a 1.12.x build Julia and fails configuration with an explicit message otherwise – a sysimage is pinned to the exact Julia build that made it and to the build host’s instruction set (cpu_target = "native"), so it is a single-host artifact by design.

What gets baked in is decided by scripts/build_sysimage.jl. The core call, verbatim:

create_sysimage(
    ["FortranBridge", "SciMLBase", "OrdinaryDiffEq", "FjKinetics"],
    project = sysimage_env,
    sysimage_path = output_path,
    precompile_execution_file = precompile_path,
    cpu_target = "native", # single-host embedding: bake the build host's ISA
)

Everything traced by precompile_execution_file (scripts/precompile.jl, plus each package’s own PrecompileTools workload) lands in the image – deliberately including both the plain-array and the view-based step_chemistry! paths, so the per-half-step call the Fortran driver evals never compiles at runtime. Expect a large file (about a gigabyte for this SciML-laden image) and a build measured in many minutes.

docs.title: Step 2: the AOT chemistry library
docs.text:
The production-shaped AOT build lives in examples/07_capstone/3_aot_kinetics/: a small Julia package (KineticsAOT) exposing Base.@ccallable kernels, compiled by PackageCompiler’s create_library into a dist/ that ships its own runtime. From that directory, run build_lib.jl with the pinned Julia; the call at its heart, verbatim (comment kept – it is the warning that cost an incident to learn):

create_library("KineticsAOT", "dist";
    lib_name = "libkinetics",
    force = true,
    header_files = ["kinetics.h"],
    incremental = false,
    filter_stdlibs = true,
    # LinearSolve (SciML closure) probes MKL_jll, a lazy artifact, at
    # image load -- without bundling it the library downloads ~570 MB
    # from the network on first init, breaking self-containedness.
    include_lazy_artifacts = true,
    precompile_execution_file = ["aot_precompile.jl"],
)

Budget for it: the non-incremental codegen of the whole closure takes on the order of an hour and tens of GB of peak compiler memory, and dist/ is ~2.5 GB. Verify self-containedness the honest way – initialize under an empty JULIA_DEPOT_PATH and a fresh home directory and confirm zero network access (Lessons, entry 5). And remember the lifecycle rule from the same page: consumers enter through the library’s exported init_julia, never the SDK’s julia_init.

The small sibling in examples/03_deployment/2_compiled_library/ (MyLib) demonstrates the identical pattern at tutorial scale; the CMake build adds its MyLib target automatically once dist/ exists.

docs.title: Step 3: the capstone figure set
docs.text:
The figures under examples/07_capstone/figures/ are rendered by one script from five CSV files; no figure is hand-edited. The pipeline:

  1. Generate the data. Run both capstone executables (ex_capstone_reacting_flow, ex_capstone_gri_ignition) and the native baseline (run_gri_native.jl, pinned binary – the figure that overlays bridge vs native inherits the baseline’s runtime). They write output/*.csv next to the examples.
  2. Render. From examples/07_capstone/figures/:
    python3 plot_capstone.py

The script’s main() renders the full set (fig1 through fig8) from ../output/*.csv, asserts each file’s column contract before drawing, and writes both PNG and PDF. A missing or stale CSV fails loudly rather than rendering an empty axis. What each figure shows, and the QA rules they are held to, are documented in examples/07_capstone/figures/FIGURES.md.

docs.title: Rebuild order after a change
docs.text: A practical note on sequencing: source changes propagate forward only. Bridge or Fortran changes need a plain rebuild plus the acceptance gates; Julia-side package changes additionally need step 1 (and step 2 if the AOT path matters to you); data-affecting changes need the examples rerun before step 3 can show anything new. Skipping a step does not fail loudly – it silently renders figures of the wrong run.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: FortranCallJulia is three worlds in one process: a Fortran application, a C bridge, and an embedded Julia runtime. The Fortran side never touches Julia APIs directly; the Julia side never sees Fortran declarations. Everything they exchange passes through the fcj_* C ABI. This page walks the layers top to bottom, then shows the full system as an interactive diagram.

docs.title: The Fortran world
docs.text:
Everything here compiles into your executable with gfortran:

  • The application layer – examples 01 through 07, from a first fcj_init call up to the two capstone executables (reacting_flow, gri_ignition).
  • julia_high_level – the object-oriented SDK: JuliaValue handles with GC-safe lifetimes, field/property navigation (%element, %property), and batch extraction (%to_fortran) for pulling whole arrays back in one call.
  • julia_low_level – the bind(c) layer of fcj_* declarations for callers that want minimal abstraction. This is where the Fast Path lives: a raw function pointer costing ~3.8 ns per call, versus ~815 ns for the generic dispatch path.

docs.title: The C bridge
docs.text:
src/bridge, eight C source files built into fcj_middleware.a, roughly 105 exported fcj_* symbols. Four concerns, four module pairs:

Module pair Owns core.c + memory.c Lifecycle (fcj_init / fcj_init_ex / exit), thread checking (check_thread()), the GC root set (fcj_map) dispatch.c + types.c Generic calls (fcj_call*, keyword arguments) and boxing (fcj_box_*) for every scalar type arrays.c + extract.c N-dimensional zero-copy wraps and deep copies; batch flow of results back to Fortran callbacks.c + accessors.c @cfunction trampolines (Julia calling Fortran) and field/property access into live objects

docs.title: The Julia world
docs.text:
• libjulia 1.12.7, pinned. The official jl_* C API, embedded in-process. The pin is load-bearing: comparison baselines must run the same Julia version the bridge embeds, or residuals are meaningless.
  • FortranBridge.jl – five modules (GCManager, FunctionRegistry, Accessors, Callbacks, Utilities) implementing the Julia side of the ABI.
  • FjKinetics.jl v0.2 – AbstractKineticsSolver with OneStepSolver (OrdinaryDiffEq, FBDF / Rodas5P) and GriSolver front ends.
  • The SciML stack, compat-pinned – Catalyst 16, OrdinaryDiffEq 6, SciMLBase 2. Pinned because unpinned drift between these packages silently degrades performance and reproducibility.
  • ChemMechSim.jl – mechanism input; supplies GRI-Mech 3.0 with 53 species and 325 reactions. Open source; the validation here used v1.2.0.

docs.title: The path of one call
docs.text:
A forward call walks four hops, with the exception flag checked after each:

Fortran bind(c) caller
  -> fcj_* entry (dispatch, boxing, root-set bookkeeping)
     -> jl_call* / jl_box_* (libjulia C API)
        -> Julia method (FortranBridge.jl or user code)

The reverse direction is symmetric: julia_callback wraps a Fortran subroutine in an @cfunction trampoline, so an OrdinaryDiffEq solver can call a Fortran right-hand side on every step. If any hop fails, the call returns an error code and get_last_error_message() carries the Julia error text back to the caller.

Delivery forms stack on top of this unchanged: the same calls run JIT (17.3 s cold start), against a sysimage (1.90 s), or AOT-compiled (first call ~12 μs) – see Deployment modes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Every headline number on this site comes from an acceptance gate that was actually run, not from design intent. Three headline gates anchor the project – the second of them itself a bundle of four internal gates. Each one compares the bridge against an independent baseline, and each one only counts when both sides run the same pinned Julia 1.12.7 – a comparison across Julia versions measures version drift, not the bridge.

docs.title: Gate 1: CJ detonation speed
docs.text:
The reacting-flow capstone (reacting_flow) simulates a Chapman–Jouguet detonation: a Fortran Euler driver with a vendored Clawpack kernel, coupled to Catalyst chemistry through Strang splitting.

Quantity Value Simulated CJ speed 7.12391 Analytic CJ speed 7.12470 Deviation 0.011%

The simulated wave speed landing within 0.011% of the analytic CJ value means the operator splitting, the bridge crossings inside it, and the Julia chemistry integrator all conserve the physics to within discretization error.

docs.title: Gate 2: bridge vs native – four internal gates, zero deviation
docs.text:
The GRI ignition case (gri_ignition) is run twice: once through the bridge and once as a native Julia baseline. Four internal acceptance gates compare the outputs.

Setting Result Julia version, both sides 1.12.7 (pinned) Gates compared 4 Deviations found 0 Residuals < 1e-12

Residuals below 1e-12 are at the level where floating-point non-associativity ends and exact agreement begins: the bridge changes nothing about the arithmetic.

Why the pin is part of the metric

An earlier comparison run once failed for a reason that had nothing to do with the bridge: a version shim silently resolved to a different Julia minor version than the one the bridge embeds, and the baseline drifted. Since then, both sides of every comparison are pinned to the same 1.12.7 binary.

docs.title: Gate 3: GRI ignition delay
docs.text:
The same machinery computes the ignition delay of a homogeneous GRI-Mech 3.0 mixture (53 species, 325 reactions):

  • t_ign = 1.1075 ms, taken as argmax |dT/dt| – the time of maximum heat-release rate, the standard sharp definition that does not depend on a threshold convention.

A physically meaningful ignition delay from a 325-reaction network is an end-to-end check: mechanism parsing (ChemMechSim.jl, open source; this validation used v1.2.0), network construction (Catalyst), stiff integration (OrdinaryDiffEq), and the data path back into Fortran arrays.

docs.title: What is FortranCallJulia?
docs.text:
FortranCallJulia embeds the Julia runtime inside a Fortran application – one process, one executable. Fortran code calls Julia through a thin C bridge (the fcj_* C ABI, about 105 symbols), and Julia calls back into Fortran through @cfunction trampolines, so a bind(c) Fortran subroutine can serve as the right-hand side of an OrdinaryDiffEq integration.

Three worlds are compiled into the final binary:

World Contents Fortran The application itself: driver, hydrodynamics, main loop. Examples 01–07, wrapped by the two-tier SDK (julia_high_level / julia_low_level). C bridge src/bridge – eight C source files built into fcj_middleware.a. Owns GC roots, argument boxing, arrays, callbacks, error checking. Julia libjulia 1.12.7 (pinned), FortranBridge.jl, FjKinetics.jl v0.2, a compat-pinned SciML stack, and ChemMechSim.jl.

docs.title: What you can do with it
docs.text:
• Call Julia from Fortran. Evaluate expressions, call functions with keyword arguments, box scalars of any type – all through fcj_* calls declared bind(c), no generated source in your build tree.
  • Pass arrays without copying. N-dimensional Fortran arrays are wrapped in place as Julia arrays; results flow back zero-copy or through batch extraction (%to_fortran copies a whole dense array in one call).
  • Call Fortran from Julia. julia_callback wraps a bind(c) subroutine into a Julia callable – for example an ODE right-hand side consumed by OrdinaryDiffEq.
  • Pick a delivery mode. The same source runs JIT-compiled, against a sysimage, or AOT-compiled – see Deployment modes.
  • Fail loudly. Every bridge call is exception-checked; a failure surfaces through get_last_error_message() instead of silently degrading into wrong answers.

docs.title: The numbers that define it
docs.text:
• Overhead. A Fast Path call – a raw C function pointer, for tight loops – costs about 3.8 ns, against roughly 815 ns for a generic typed call (100k-iteration averages).
  • Startup ladder. JIT 17.3 s from cold start to first result; a sysimage cuts that to 1.90 s; the AOT build answers its first call in about 12 μs, approaching the native baseline.
  • Correctness. CJ detonation speed 7.12391 vs the analytic 7.12470 (0.011% deviation); bridge vs native shows 0 deviation across four acceptance gates; GRI ignition delay t_ign = 1.1075 ms. Details and context in Validation.

docs.title: Why Fortran and Julia?
docs.text: Most scientific code is not greenfield. The situation this project was built for: a mature Fortran hydrodynamics code that is trusted, fast, and expensive to touch – sitting next to a Julia solver ecosystem that keeps producing tools Fortran has no equivalent of. FortranCallJulia’s answer is to stop choosing. Keep the hydrodynamics in Fortran, take the solver ecology from Julia, couple both in one process.

docs.title: What stays in Fortran
docs.text:
• The physics driver. Decades-validated numerics with existing verification baselines. A rewrite would reset that trust for zero physical gain.
  • The main loop and I/O. Time stepping, mesh management, checkpointing, HPC launcher integration – the parts where the Fortran toolchain is already proven.
  • The deployment shape. The final artifact is still one executable, compiled by gfortran, that a cluster scheduler can run unchanged. Julia is linked in, not shipped alongside.

docs.title: What comes from Julia
docs.text:
• A live stiff-ODE ecosystem. OrdinaryDiffEq solvers (FBDF, Rodas5P) integrate stiff chemistry without hand-rolled implicit integrators, and improvements arrive as package updates.
  • Reaction kinetics as code. Catalyst builds the reaction network; GRI-Mech 3.0 – 53 species, 325 reactions – is consumed through ChemMechSim.jl (open source; the validation here used v1.2.0).
  • Composability without churn on the Fortran side. A new solver, a new package version, a new model – the Fortran code keeps calling the same fcj_* entry points.

docs.title: The coupling, in one sentence of numerics
docs.text: The reacting-flow capstone couples an explicit Fortran Euler step (a Clawpack kernel) with a stiff Julia chemistry step through Strang splitting – half a hydro step, then a full chemistry step, then half a hydro step – which keeps second-order accuracy in time while each world integrates with the method that suits it.

docs.title: Why a C bridge in the middle
docs.text:
Julia’s only stable embedding surface is its C API: libjulia and the jl_* functions. The bridge in src/bridge is the single place that talks to that API, so the rest of the system never does. Concentrating the C there buys three things:

  1. GC safety. Every object handed to Fortran is entered into a C-side root set (fcj_map) that outlives Julia’s collector, then released explicitly.
  2. Error discipline. Every call is exception-checked; failures return an error code and human-readable text via get_last_error_message().
  3. A stable, narrow ABI. Roughly 105 fcj_* symbols – small enough to audit, stable enough that Fortran and Julia can evolve independently on either side.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: The bridge is not free of constraints: bridge calls are pinned to the thread that initialized Julia, the array channel supports Float64 / ComplexF64 (scalars are all-type), and the supported platform is Linux with gcc/gfortran. The full list is in Known limitations; the design decisions behind it continue in Architecture.

docs.title: Arrays and callbacks
docs.text: Scalars crossed the bridge on Your first call; real computing moves arrays and needs control flow in both directions. This page is the remaining data plumbing: arrays into Julia without copying, arrays back out in one call, and a bind(c) Fortran subroutine driven from Julia as a right-hand side. All of it sits on the two SDKs of Two SDKs, two speeds.

docs.title: Arrays in: zero-copy wrap or deep copy
docs.text:
Two rank-generic functions decide how an array crosses, and they differ only in memory ownership. Both are single assumed-rank entry points that read the extents from size(arr, k) – there is no caller-supplied length that could disagree with the array – and both take any rank from 1 to 16 of contiguous real(kind=8) data.

julia_wrap_array(arr) julia_copy_array(arr) What Julia gets an Array{Float64,N} header pointing at your memory a fresh Array{Float64,N}, data memcpy’d in Data motion none: the wrap builds a header, not a payload one full copy (and another if you copy results back) Julia-side writes land in your Fortran array, immediately land in Julia’s copy Ownership yours; Julia never frees the memory Julia’s, GC-managed Reach for it when in-place kernels, big grids, hot loops the Julia side keeps the array, or you want the aliasing gone

Both reject loudly instead of guessing: a rank above 16, any zero extent (c_loc on a zero-sized array is illegal), or a non-contiguous actual argument each yields an invalid JuliaValue plus a diagnostic on error_unit.

The wrap in action, from examples/01_basics/2_zero_copy_arrays.f90:

    ! 2. Box the Fortran Array into a Julia Object
    !    This creates a Julia Array header pointing to the EXISTING Fortran memory.
    !    NO DATA COPY happens here. Extents are derived from size() by the SDK.
    dummy = julia_wrap_array(simulation_grid)

    ! 3. Call Julia Function with the Array
    !    Julia sees a standard Matrix{Float64}.
    !    Any changes Julia makes are written directly to 'simulation_grid'.
    !    ExamplesLib.update_simulation_state!(grid, dt)
    res = julia%call("ExamplesLib.update_simulation_state!", dummy, 0.5d0)

    ! 4. Verify Changes in Fortran
    print *, "After Julia Update:"
    print *, "Grid(1,1) [Expected > 0]: ", simulation_grid(1,1)
    print *, "Grid(50,50):              ", simulation_grid(50,50)

simulation_grid started at zero; after the call its elements are not. That is the proof of zero-copy – had a copy happened, the Fortran array would still read 0.0. One rule comes with the wrap: the header points at your memory and the ownership flag says Julia will not free it, so keeping that memory alive and in place, for as long as any handle can still reach it, is your side of the bargain.

N-dimensional means it: the rank is not capped at 2 or 3. The same wrap through the raw C ABI, from examples/01_basics/2_arrays.f90:

    ! --- 3. Hypermatrix (4D, zero-copy through the rank-generic API) ---
    ! The high-level SDK form is simply  vec_obj = julia_wrap_array(hyper)
    ! (extents derived from size()); here we exercise the raw C form and
    ! verify the wrap via introspection.
    hyper = 0.0d0
    raw_ptr = c_loc(hyper)
    dims(1:4) = [2_c_long, 3_c_long, 4_c_long, 5_c_long]
    wrapped_ptr = fcj_wrap_array(raw_ptr, 4_c_long, dims)
    mat_obj%ptr = fcj_retain(wrapped_ptr)
    print *, "  3. Rank-4 wrap: ndims=", mat_obj%ndims(), &
             " sizes=", (mat_obj%size_dim(k), k=1,4)

The deep copy is the same call shape with different economics. Both fragments below run on a 3000 x 3000 matrix (about 72 MB), from examples/04_performance/3_memory_transfer.f90:

    ! Step 1: Explicit Deep Copy to Julia
    wrapped_array = julia_copy_array(matrix)
    ! Step 2: Call function (returns new array)
    res = julia%call("perf_scale_matrix", wrapped_array, 2.0d0)

    ! Step 1: Wrap (O(1))
    ! The rank-generic wrapper derives the extents from size()
    wrapped_array = julia_wrap_array(matrix)

    ! Step 2: Call In-Place Function
    ! We pass the wrapped array. No data moves.
    res = julia%call("perf_scale_matrix_bang", wrapped_array, 2.0d0)

docs.title: Arrays out: navigate, then copy once
docs.text:
Results come back as handles. Two accessors navigate a result object, and one call moves the data:

  • %element(i) – 1-based linear indexing, returns a retained handle.
  • %property(name) (and its sibling %get_field(name)) – named access through Base.getproperty: struct fields, NamedTuple keys, solver solution objects.
  • %to_fortran(buf, n) – copies a dense array into your Fortran buffer in one call; the real and complex overloads resolve by the buffer type.

From examples/06_sciml/2_batch_data.f90 (fail is that example’s local abort helper):

    d = julia_eval(' (a = [7.0,8.0,9.0],) ')
    if (.not. d%is_valid()) &
        call fail('julia_eval NamedTuple failed')
    a = d%property("a")
    if (.not. a%is_valid()) &
        call fail('property("a") failed: ' // get_last_error_message())
    rc = a%to_fortran(rbuf, 3_c_int64_t)
    if (rc /= 0) &
        call fail('to_fortran on NamedTuple property failed: ' // get_last_error_message())

The error idiom is the house style from Your first call: check the handle or the return code, and get_last_error_message() carries the Julia-side text. An out-of-bounds %element(5) on a two-element vector, for instance, returns an invalid handle and populates the message.

Batch extraction is also the cheap way across. Every per-element access is a bridge hop; %to_fortran is one hop for the whole array. The same arithmetic says: when a loop could run on either side, run it in Julia and cross once with an array – examples/04_performance/4_access_patterns.f90 measures exactly that trade at a million elements.

docs.title: Callbacks: Fortran as a right-hand side
docs.text:
Arrays move data; callbacks hand control to Fortran. julia_callback wraps a bind(c) subroutine pointer into a Julia callable f(du, u, p, t) – the signature DifferentialEquations-style solvers expect – so the solver calls into your Fortran on every step. The callable ccalls your subroutine, and a context pointer you supply at creation reaches it untouched on every invocation.

The subroutine signs a six-argument contract. This one, from examples/06_sciml/1_callback.f90, is a stateless exponential decay du = -k*u:

    subroutine rhs(ctx, n, u, du, t, err) bind(c)
        type(c_ptr), value, intent(in) :: ctx        ! unused (stateless RHS)
        integer(kind=c_int64_t), value, intent(in) :: n
        type(c_ptr), value, intent(in) :: u, du
        real(kind=c_double), value, intent(in) :: t  ! unused (autonomous RHS)
        integer(kind=c_int), intent(out) :: err

        real(kind=c_double), pointer :: u_arr(:), du_arr(:)
        integer :: i

        err = 0_c_int
        if (n <= 0_c_int64_t) return
        call c_f_pointer(u, u_arr, [int(n)])
        call c_f_pointer(du, du_arr, [int(n)])
        do i = 1, int(n)
            du_arr(i) = -K_DECAY * u_arr(i)
        end do
    end subroutine rhs

Three properties of that contract:

  • u and du are raw pointers into Julia’s arrays – the zero-copy channel above, in reverse. You read u and write du in place, n elements each; nothing is marshalled per step.
  • err is the error path. Return nonzero and the Julia side throws; the bridge catches the exception and it surfaces at the Fortran call site through get_last_error_message(). No Fortran failure crosses silently.
  • ctx is yours – any type(c_ptr) you passed at creation, handed back on every call (ignored by this stateless RHS).

Wiring it up, same example:

    ! 2. Wrap the bind(c) RHS into a Julia callable (already retained)
    fn = c_funloc(rhs)
    cb = julia_callback(fn, c_null_ptr)
    if (.not. cb%is_valid()) then
        write (error_unit, '(A)') 'FATAL: julia_callback failed: ' // get_last_error_message()
        stop 1
    end if

    ! 3. Box f's arguments: du (Float64 vector workspace, zero-copy),
    !    u = [1.0], p = 0.0, t = 0.0 (p is ignored by the bridge closure)
    du_f(1) = 0.0_c_double
    u_f(1) = 1.0_c_double
    du_boxed = julia_wrap_array(du_f)
    u_boxed = julia_wrap_array(u_f)
    p_boxed = julia_box_real(0.0_c_double)
    t_boxed = julia_box_real(0.0_c_double)
    if (.not. du_boxed%is_valid() .or. .not. u_boxed%is_valid()) then
        write (error_unit, '(A)') 'FATAL: boxing du/u failed'
        stop 1
    end if

    ! 4. Invoke the Julia callable f(du, u, p, t); it ccalls back into
    !    rhs, which writes du in place.
    res = cb%call_value(du_boxed, u_boxed, p_boxed, t_boxed)

After call_value, du_f(1) already holds -K_DECAY * 1.0: the RHS wrote straight into the Fortran array that was wrapped as du. The bridge also binds the callable to Main.FJ_CALLBACK, so solver code assembled with julia_eval_string can reach it by name. The end-to-end version – a harmonic oscillator integrated with Tsit5, checked to about 1e-9 against the analytic solution – is examples/06_sciml/3_sciml_demo.f90.

Both directions ride trampolines. This one boxes your bind(c) address as an opaque pointer and closes over it in Julia. In the other direction, get_function_pointer has the bridge generate an @cfunction trampoline rooted in Main, handing Fortran a raw C pointer to a Julia function at ~3.8 ns per call; that path and its hard edges belong to Two SDKs, two speeds.

docs.title: The rules both channels share
docs.text:
1. One thread. Every bridge call – a wrap, an extraction, a callback invocation – runs on the thread that initialized the runtime. A callback is no exception: the solver executes on the thread that called it, which in this bridge is always the init thread.
  2. Array element types are Float64 and ComplexF64, only. Wraps take contiguous real(c_double); %to_fortran fills a real or complex buffer. Scalars are not so bounded – every scalar type boxes. This is a known limit, tracked in Known limitations.
  3. Crossings are the budget, not calls. A generic call costs ~815 ns and a Fast Path call ~3.8 ns (100k-iteration averages); either is noise next to real solver work. But a per-element loop that crosses the bridge a million times pays the hop a million times. Move the loop into one side; do not move the elements across.

docs.title: Bring your own kinetics
docs.text:
The capstone does not hardcode its chemistry. The Fortran driver advances cells through FjKinetics, the small Julia package at examples/07_capstone/FjKinetics/, whose v0.2 puts every mechanism behind one interface – so the flow solver never learns what chemistry it is burning. Bringing your own kinetics comes in two tiers:

  1. Use ChemMechSim as-is. An open-source Julia package that loads Cantera-YAML reaction mechanisms; the capstone’s GRI-Mech 3.0 benchmark runs on it unchanged.
  2. Implement AbstractKineticsSolver. Two methods, one contract – your mechanism drops in behind the same Fortran call.

docs.title: The contract: AbstractKineticsSolver
docs.text:
The base type and its meaning, verbatim from examples/07_capstone/FjKinetics/src/FjKinetics.jl:

"""
    AbstractKineticsSolver

Common base of the chemistry solvers. The mechanism-agnostic contract is
[`step_chemistry!`](@ref)(solver, Y, T, rho, dt): `Y` is `ncell x nspec`
species MASS fractions in the solver's species order, `T` cell temperatures,
`rho` cell densities; all are advanced in place by `dt`.
"""
abstract type AbstractKineticsSolver end

A solver is that base plus two methods. All four definitions below are verbatim from the same file (the two nspecies lines and the two step_chemistry! signatures sit at different points in it; bodies elided):

nspecies(ks::KineticsSolver) = ks.nspec
nspecies(gs::GriSolver) = gs.nspec

function step_chemistry!(ks::KineticsSolver, Y::AbstractMatrix{<:Real},
                         T::AbstractVector{<:Real}, rho::AbstractVector{<:Real},
                         dt::Real)

function step_chemistry!(gs::GriSolver, Y::AbstractMatrix{<:Real},
                         T::AbstractVector{<:Real}, rho::AbstractVector{<:Real},
                         dt::Real)

Read the contract off those names:

Argument Meaning Y ncell x nspec species mass fractions in the solver’s species order, advanced in place T cell temperatures, advanced in place rho cell densities; part of the contract even when a mechanism ignores it – the single-step one does, GRI-Mech 3.0 needs it dt how far every cell is advanced nspecies(solver) the nspec columns the Fortran side packs per cell

FjKinetics v0.2 ships two solvers under the base: OneStepSolver (an alias of KineticsSolver – the single-step Arrhenius mechanism of the reacting-flow capstone) and GriSolver (a full mechanism through ChemMechSim).

docs.title: Tier 1: ChemMechSim and the GRI-Mech 3.0 capstone
docs.text:
ChemMechSim.jl is an open-source Julia package for Cantera-YAML reaction mechanisms; it bundles GRI-Mech 3.0 itself (53 species, 325 reactions) at examples/mechanism/gri30.yaml inside the ChemMechSim package – that path is in the package, not in this repository. One version note before you compare digits: the General registry currently carries v1.0.0 while the repository is at v1.2.0, and every validation number on this site was produced against v1.2.0 – check which one your environment actually resolved.

Setup is one script. scripts/install_sciml_env.jl – run with the same Julia 1.12.x the bridge embeds – creates the scratch environment scripts/sysimage_env and develops FortranBridge, FjKinetics, and your ChemMechSim checkout into it (CHEMMECHSIM_PATH overrides where the checkout lives). The capstone executables probe for that environment at startup; FJ_KINETICS_PROJECT redirects the probe.

Then build the examples and generate the native baseline first (run_gri_native.jl, under the pinned Julia – it refuses to run under a version shim, because a drifting baseline fails the gates while wrongly blaming the bridge). The bridge side of the benchmark, from examples/07_capstone/2_gri_ignition.f90 – the whole chemistry driver kept in one eval, so a Julia-side throw surfaces as an invalid result with the reason in get_last_error_message():

    call julia_eval_string( &
        'function fj_gri_run() :: NamedTuple' // new_line('a') // &
        '    gs = FjKinetics.build_gri30_kinetics()' // new_line('a') // &
        '    return FjKinetics.run_gri_ignition(gs)' // new_line('a') // &
        'end')
    res = dummy%call('fj_gri_run')
    if (.not. res%is_valid()) &
        call fail('fj_gri_run failed: ' // get_last_error_message())

The solution’s arrays come back in bulk copies – ts (2001 points), T (2001), and the 4 x 2001 mole-fraction matrix X flattened into one buffer: one %to_fortran per array, zero per-element bridge traffic. The ts and X legs, verbatim:

    v = res%property('ts')
    if (.not. v%is_valid()) call fail('property ts: ' // get_last_error_message())
    rc = v%to_fortran(ts, int(NSAMPLE, kind=c_int64_t))
    if (rc /= 0) call fail('to_fortran ts: ' // get_last_error_message())

    ! Matrix{Float64} 4x2001, bulk-copied into the flat buffer
    v = res%property('X')
    if (.not. v%is_valid()) call fail('property X: ' // get_last_error_message())
    rc = v%to_fortran(Xflat, int(NSP_OUT * NSAMPLE, kind=c_int64_t))
    if (rc /= 0) call fail('to_fortran X: ' // get_last_error_message())

(The T leg between them is the same shape again.) Fortran then owns the verdict – the ignition criterion is computed on the extracted arrays, the same one the validation script uses:

    do k = 1, NSAMPLE - 1
        dtdt(k) = abs((T(k + 1) - T(k)) / (ts(k + 1) - ts(k)))
    end do
    imax = maxloc(dtdt, 1)          ! first occurrence, like Julia's argmax
    t_ign_f = ts(imax + 1)

Acceptance is four gates against the native run – the Fortran-computed t_ign, the extracted T_end, and two X spot values that pin the column-major matrix layout – each within a relative 1e-8 (Validation). The headline that comes out: t_ign = 1.1075 ms for stoichiometric CH4/air at 1500 K and 1 atm, constant-volume adiabatic, the delay taken at argmax |dT/dt|.

Pin your environment before blaming anything. FjKinetics’ [compat] pins the solve stack – Catalyst ~16.2, OrdinaryDiffEq ~6.111, SciMLBase ~2.155 – because an unpinned environment once drifted onto the OrdinaryDiffEq 7.x line, whose step-size controller degraded the per-cell reinit!/step! pattern by about 700x per grid cell (a frozen cell cost 982 internal steps instead of 1). If per-cell chemistry suddenly crawls, check the resolve first; the bridge is the usual suspect and usually innocent.

docs.title: Tier 2: implement the interface
docs.text:
Your mechanism becomes a subtype plus the two methods. The rules that keep it drop-in:

  1. Mirror the argument shapes exactly (Y::AbstractMatrix{<:Real}, T/rho::AbstractVector{<:Real}, dt::Real): the capstone passes wrapped Fortran memory and views of it, and dispatch lands on your concrete type.
  2. Validate loudly, like the built-ins. The guard pair from the KineticsSolver method, verbatim:
    size(Y, 1) == ncell && size(Y, 2) == ks.nspec && length(rho) == ncell ||
        error("step_chemistry!: Y must be $(ncell)x$(ks.nspec), rho $(ncell)")
    dt > 0 || error("step_chemistry!: dt must be positive, got $dt")
  1. Advance in place; return an admissible state. If you return mass fractions, keep Y >= 0 and sum(Y) == 1 – GriSolver clamps tolerance-level negative concentrations (trace species undershooting at abstol) before closing the sum, because a microscopically negative mass fraction fed back into a compressible flow solver is a real hazard.
  2. Throwing is allowed on this path. The bridge catches the exception and the reason surfaces at the Fortran call site through get_last_error_message(). The raw function-pointer route of Two SDKs, two speeds is the one path where the called body must not throw.
  3. rho is part of the contract even if your mechanism ignores it; Fortran always packs it.

The Fortran side never changes. The capstone wraps its persistent cell buffers once, and every Strang half-step is ONE batched call over the active cells – from examples/07_capstone/1_reacting_flow.f90 (the packing loop above it is elided):

            write (dts, '(es24.16)') dt_half
            write (expr, '(a,i0,a,i0,a,i0,a)') &
                'FjKinetics.step_chemistry!(FJ_KS, view(FJ_Y,1:', n_act, &
                ',:), view(FJ_T,1:', n_act, '), view(FJ_RHO,1:', n_act, &
                '), ' // trim(dts) // ')'
            v_res = julia_eval(trim(expr))

Swap what FJ_KS is bound to and that same line advances 2 species or 53: the mechanism lives entirely on the Julia side of the view.
